🇺🇸 US retailers: Target - Switch 2 console: check stock Amazon - Switch 2 console: check stock - Switch 2 Pro controller: check stock Best Buy - Switch 2 console: check stock - Switch 2 Pro controller: check stock ---------------------------------- 🇬🇧 UK retailers: Amazon - Switch 2 console: check stock - Switch 2 Pro controller: check stock Smyths Toys - Switch 2 console: check stock - Switch 2 Pro controller: check stock ---------------------------------- Latest LIVE updates
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has launched, and it's glorious. But the real challenge isn't saving Hyrule as Link; it's finding a restock of the Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition Nintendo Switch 2 console.
Restocks are rolling out — Target and Nintendo recently dropped fresh chances to grab the hard-to-find console — and with Nintendo promising more stock is on the way, I'm bringing you the latest stock updates.
As of now, there is no Zelda Switch 2 restock available . However, multiple retailers are prioritizing in-store restocks (Best Buy, Walmart, GameStop), so if you can, be sure to check your nearest locations.
I've been covering pre-order events and restocks at Tom's Guide for more than five years, and know how to secure in-demand items. Below are all the links you need, alongside live updates on Zelda Switch 2 restocks.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has been remade for the Nintendo Switch 2. One of the N64's most beloved games has been completely overhauled to celebrate the franchise's 40th Anniversary. The remake offers truly stunning visuals with 4K graphics, overhauled controls, and reworked puzzles.
I'm a Senior Entertainment Editor at Tom's Guide and a more recent convert to The Legend of Zelda series. Breath of the Wild on Switch 1 was my first Zelda experience, and I can't wait to finally play Ocarina of Time.
I've been checking all the retailers every so often, but I've just done a full retailer sweep to see what's available.
A whole lot of nearly nothing.
The one place I was able to see was on Target. There's a button that will show you stores with stock near you. For me, it was one store with one console in stock about 10 miles away.
If you have gas in the car and a minute, this might be the way to get your special Switch 2.
If you didn't know there are two versions of the cover art for the Ocarina of Time remake. One with foil texture and one without.
Apparently, the retails have all swapped out the foil cover on their listings for the standard edition.
You may get lucky if you try your luck in-store, but online it appears out of stock.
GameStop is showing the Zelda console as out of stock but the Pro Controller might still be available. However, the retailer has been pushing in-store so you won't be able to get it on the website.
I called my local GameStop and they were out of stock, but you might have better luck with your closest store.
I just did a sweep through the retailers, and it looks like the only thing available is the 40th anniversary Pro Controller for $213.99 at Walmart , which is double the normal $99 price, but cheaper than what I'm seeing on Best Buy (showing as sold out).
Nothing to report at present, Target has now returned to "sold out", though perhaps we'll see a third restock later today, meanwhile no signs of any stock at Walmart so the rumors are unfortunately looking increasingly unlikely. In-store remains your chance to find a Zelda Switch 2 , so if you live locally to a retailer, it's worth trying your luck. Meanwhile, my day is winding down, but I'll be handing over to a colleague shortly, to make sure you don't miss any restocks.
Quick update on the Target situation, I'm no longer seeing the "add to cart" button, but it does direct me to "show in-store stock" with at least one location popping up claiming to have stock nearby. It would seem all the online inventory has been snapped up, but I would still recommend checking for now, you could get lucky. And Target has restocked online twice now, could it go for a third?
I didn't see this one coming, but the "add to cart" button has just returned on Target, so get over there and see if you can secure a Zelda Switch 2 as it looks like stock is returning at the retailer!
All eyes are on Walmart at present, there are rumors flying around they will restock the Zelda Switch 2 today, but so far nothing. Remember, as I keep saying, there's no confirmation here, but restock rumors often prove to have some truth to them, so fingers firmly crossed the noise around Walmart amounts to a drop.
Well, after about an hour, I'm not seeing any signs of available stock at Target, even with a lot of refreshes, so I feel pretty confident saying the retailer is once again sold out . Hopefully you were able to grab one in this latest Zelda Switch 2 restock. If not, don't worry, I'm still here tracking stock levels across retailers. Remember, Walmart is rumored to drop next.
Target was the big one today, and after restocking in the very early morning hours, I wondered if that would be the retailer sold out again, but a second restock has appeared online. The console is going to sell out fast, so get over there, and even if you get a "sold out" message at first, keep trying, as more stock could appear.
No time for talking, the Zelda Switch 2 is IN STOCK at Target, go grab yours!!!
Last night after a busy day of restock tracking, I finally got to sink my teeth into The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and while I'm very early in my quest, my first impressions are that it's a glorious remake.
Our reviewer, Anthony Spadafora, had a similar experience, calling it "even better than my childhood memories." You can read his full Ocarina of Time review if you're looking to fill some time until we have more restock news to bring you.
Rumors have been flying around this week that Walmart could restock the Zelda Switch 2 from November 6 (aka today). This is based on an unverified leak of an internal document suggesting that the national retailer was gearing up for a restock. Again, this is all unconfirmed, but it's the retailer to watch right now, and it has already this week restocked in-store, so could an online drop follow today?
One of the big themes this week has been retailers opting for in-store restocks rather than dropping stock online.
I've just checked some local Target stores, and the retailer's online tracker is telling me there is Zelda Switch 2's available at nearby locations. However it's very limited ("only 1 left"), and these in-store stock trackers aren't always updated in realtime, so even if it tells you there's stock there's no guarantees.
Still, if you've got your heart set on securing a Zelda Switch 2, and have a Target store within reasonable distance (I wouldn't recommend a lengthy roadtrip), then getting down to your nearest location might be your best chance of getting one.
It looks like Target opted for a late-night online restock based on what I've seen on social media, so if you're still on the hunt for a Zelda Switch 2, that's the place to check now. But I'm seeing conflicting reports, with some users claiming that no stock was available, so I'll keep watching the retailer for signs of more stock.
Good morning! Rory here, it's a new day, and I'm back online to track Zelda Switch 2 restock across retailers. Today (Nov. 6) is set to be a big day with at least one online restock confirmed at Target, and there could be more on the way, too.

articles.title_orig: President Peña skips Senate impeachment trial as Paraguay reels from Ueno bank collapse
articles.title_zh: President Peña skips Senate impeachment trial as Paraguay reels from Ueno bank collapse
articles.content_orig:
Paraguay's President Santiago PeÃ±a has announced his resignation following a political crisis sparked by the collapse of a bank linked to him.
"I want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed," he said in a video message on social media. "It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me."
The crisis erupted after Ueno Bank entered an insolvency process, which froze all operations. Lawmakers accused PeÃ±a, who was a shareholder until last year in the company that owned the bank, of conflicts of interest and misconduct.
PeÃ±a rejected suggestions of impropriety. His resignation came as Paraguay's lower house of congress voted in favour of pursuing an impeachment trial.
Photos taken near Paraguay's Congress building on Thursday show police officers clashing with protesters demanding PeÃ±a be removed from office.
Paraguay's congress must approve the resignation of a president. But a special session convened on Thursday to address his resignation was adjourned in favour of continuing with the impeachment process.
Congress has scheduled a special session for Friday, when PeÃ±a is expected to present his defence, according to Reuters news agency.
In a post on X, PeÃ±a confirmed he would appear for Senate impeachment proceedings, adding that he would do so to "exercise my right to a defence".
He wrote: "I will provide the information requested of me. Citizens deserve to know the truth, without cover-ups and without anyone being above the law."
PeÃ±a earlier said his resignation was to protect stability, social peace and democratic institutions.
Ueno Bank has said it has about three million customers, equivalent to about 60% of Paraguay's adult population.
It held pensions and some other public funds and, after its collapse earlier this week, millions could not access their accounts.
The central bank seized the digital lender, and people took to the streets protesting and demanding PeÃ±a's resignation.
A new president of the Central Bank of Paraguay has been appointed and Congress has approved a process to pay depositors.
Protesters gathered near the Paraguayan Congress on Thursday
PeÃ±a won election in 2023 representing Paraguay's ruling conservative Colorado Party, beating a centre-left challenger.
The Colorado party dropped impeachment proceedings against Vice President Pedro Alliana, who is next in line for the presidency after PeÃ±a.

articles.title_orig: Hegseth calls US-Iran war a 'courageous and historic effort'
articles.title_zh: Hegseth calls US-Iran war a 'courageous and historic effort'
articles.content_orig:
Iran has stepped up diplomatic efforts amid suggestions by United States President Donald Trump that the US could resume full-scale strikes on Iran.
The US news website Axios quoted a US official saying that US Central Command (CENTCOM) was preparing for the resumption of major military operations in Iran, and that it was just waiting on orders from Washington. On Thursday, Trump told reporters the US may have to “destroy” the rest of Iran, adding that people will “know soon enough” if he acts.
Tehran’s intensified diplomatic push comes after Iran downed two US reconnaissance drones near Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, which the US struck earlier this week. Iran says it will retaliate if the US resumes larger strikes.
On Thursday, Iran offered the US a new nuclear and peace proposal via Qatari mediators, to be discussed only after Washington meets Tehran’s seven demands, a senior Iranian official told Reuters. The US is examining the proposal, Reuters reported.
Iran has made meeting its seven demands a condition for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and restarting peace talks, including on its nuclear programme. The demands include the lifting of sanctions on Iran, the unfreezing of Iranian assets and the end to the US naval blockade of its ports in and around the Strait of Hormuz, among other things.
It has also stepped up ties with Russia, with its top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, travelling to Moscow for talks on Thursday. During that visit, Rezaei said: “On the issue of diplomacy, we have announced seven conditions ⁠to the Americans. As long as they do ⁠not execute our seven conditions, we will neither open the Strait of Hormuz nor have negotiations.”
Meanwhile, the US has insisted a deal on Iran’s nuclear capacity must be part of any ceasefire agreement before wider peace talks can restart.
On Thursday, Rezaei met with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin to deliver a message from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Iranian state media did not elaborate on ⁠the contents of the message.
Rezaei called it “an extremely important exchange” according to remarks reported by the Iranian embassy, but also did not give further details.
However, The Financial Times reported that Russia previously agreed to supply Iran with 90 helicopter-mounted launchers for precision-guided missiles, despite needing its own weapons for the Ukraine war. The newspaper cited a Russian defence manufacturer’s production schedule for 2024 and 2025, which it has examined, showing an order for helicopter-mounted launchers being assigned a code used to refer to Iran in Russian defence documents.
Relations between Russia and Iran have deepened since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and during the US-Israeli war on Iran that saw the two countries become the most heavily sanctioned in the world. Iran has provided Shahed drones, which Russia has modified and used heavily against Ukraine.
In return, Russia has also reportedly helped Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles, sold it Verba shoulder-launched anti-air missiles and shared information with Tehran potentially relevant to nuclear weapons.
“It is indicative of Russia’s willingness to continue supplying Iran despite its own wartime demands and with far less concern about Western objections than in the past,” Nicole Grajewski, a non-resident scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told the FT.
In early October, Putin said Russia was prepared to take part in mediation to bring an end to the war .
Images released by the Kremlin showed its foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov and chief of the Russian military intelligence, Igor Kostyukov, attending a meeting with Iran’s security chief alongside Putin.
The meeting also strengthened Iran’s economic ties with Russia.
“During the meeting with Mr Vladimir Putin, discussions were held regarding the construction of gas pipelines from Russia to Iran,” said Rezaei, Iranian state TV reported.
He said the gas pipelines would address Iran’s gas shortages and facilitate the sale of Russian energy to neighbouring countries.
Tehran said Iran’s natural gas refineries had been hit during the most intense phase of US-Israeli strikes on Iran earlier this year, which lasted 40 days.
Separately, Russia’s Foreign Ministry advised citizens against travel to Iran “In light of the remaining risks of a new escalation around Iran”.
During the most intense fighting of the war, Iran struck bases in Gulf countries hosting US military assets, as well as civil and energy facilities and infrastructure.
Senior Iranian officials have repeatedly warned that any state helping the US to target the Islamic republic will be a “legitimate target” should US attacks resume.
On Thursday, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held phone calls with several Gulf leaders, including the foreign minister of the UAE, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
They discussed regional developments as well as diplomatic efforts for stability in the region, according to Araghchi’s Telegram channel.
Araghchi spoke with Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud about efforts to improve security and stability in the region, according to the Saudi foreign ministry.
Araghchi also discussed de-escalation efforts with the foreign ministers of Kuwait and Turkiye.
In a separate call, Araghchi talked with Qatar’s Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani about coordinating to reduce tensions, the Qatari foreign ministry said.
Sheikh Mohammed stressed support for efforts to secure freedom of maritime navigation.
In a statement, Oman’s foreign ministry said the safety of passage through the Strait of Hormuz was a main topic of discussions, in a call between Araghchi and Oman’s foreign minister.
Iran continues to tightly control shipping lanes through the strait, where several ships have been damaged in recent days. It has granted exemptions to shipping restrictions to Iraq and Qatar, in the Gulf region, as well as to India and China.
Despite his Republican Party suffering a drubbing in this week’s US midterm elections – largely because of public anger over the war on Iran and the resulting rise in energy prices – US President Donald Trump has refused to rule out further strikes on Iran.
On Thursday, Trump told reporters at the Oval Office that he may have to “destroy the rest” of Iran.
Former Iranian diplomat Hadi Afghahi told Al Jazeera that Tehran can ease the path to a settlement if the US also shows flexibility. He argued that Trump “really does not want to go to war, because war again will cost him more”. However, the US president’s next move is unpredictable, observers say.
Afghahi cautioned that Trump “is still surrounded by a group of hawks”, including the energy and treasury secretaries.
Trump has shown willingness to engage in diplomacy, however. Qatar’s ⁠Emir ⁠Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad ⁠Al Thani discussed diplomatic ⁠efforts to ease regional tensions in a ‌phone call with Trump on Friday, according to the Qatari Emiri Diwan.
The leaders reviewed international diplomatic efforts, including the Doha-led mediation efforts to support negotiations in recent weeks, in a bid to reach “a comprehensive agreement that puts an end to the crisis”, the Diwan said in a statement.
Tehran warned it will retaliate on a wider scale than it has done so far if the US resumes the war. It has also said talks will become unfeasible.
Iranian officials said Iran has the capacity to strike further than the Gulf using weapons manufactured in Iran.
On Thursday, a spokesman for the Supreme Advisor to the Commander of the Aerospace Force of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said: “In the event of a new aggression, any country or force that helps America attack Iran can be a legitimate target of the Islamic Republic.”

articles.title_orig: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values
articles.title_zh: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values
articles.content_orig:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.
On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.
But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday, ending the day up 1.1%, partly reversing some of its 5.5% fall.
The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.
Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.
However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.
The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.
In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.
In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.
The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.
A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.
US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.
Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.
"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.
"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."
Pierre BaquÃ©, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure.
"The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said.
"We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.
"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."
Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.
And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.
Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September .
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.
Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.
"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

articles.title_orig: How Elon Musk Frittered Away Nearly $500 Million on the Midterm Elections
articles.title_zh: How Elon Musk Frittered Away Nearly $500 Million on the Midterm Elections
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX and Tesla shares declined by about 9% and 11%, respectively, on Thursday afternoon with investors concerned that Elon Musk could face new congressional probes — and his companies stricter regulation — following the U.S. midterm elections.
The declines, which correlated with a broader tech sell-off , brought aggregate market cap losses for SpaceX and Tesla to over $420 billion since Tuesday's close.
Musk's wealth, which had topped $1 trillion after SpaceX's initial public offering in June, is now down below $800 billion, having dropped about $90 billion in the past week, according to Forbes . He is still the richest man in the world.
Musk was the biggest donor to GOP candidates and causes in the midterms, with his financial contributions exceeding $470 million , the Financial Times first reported.
Despite his bolstering the GOP war chest, most of the candidates Musk backed lost their races .
Democrats won control of both the House and Senate. And in Texas, where both Tesla and SpaceX are headquartered, Democrats Sen.-elect James Talarico and Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa beat longtime Musk allies, state Attorney General Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott.
Deutsche Bank analysts wrote in a note out on Wednesday, "While policy is naturally hard to predict, we could envision SpaceX facing some incremental headwinds in this type of backdrop."
Gov.-elect Hinojosa "made data centers a major campaign issue," the analysts noted, calling for "a moratorium on new approvals until the legislature passes stronger protections on water use, electricity costs, local control, and incentives," and criticizing tax breaks for large facilities.
Tesla and SpaceX are both building out AI infrastructure in Texas, and are planning to build Terafab, a massive facility, which will include a data center and sprawling semiconductor factory, in Grimes County, Texas.
SpaceX also plans to build out a "supercomputer" at its Starbase, Texas, launch facility and company town, according to company job listings .
Deutsche Bank analysts also wrote that SpaceX's Texas compute capacity could now be at risk of delays. Capital expenditures by the company may need to increase to meet the requirements of tighter, anticipated regulations around data center buildout, the analysts wrote.
Musk and SpaceX have been instructed to preserve records concerning restrictions imposed on a military version of the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, CNN first reported , citing an aide to a Democratic senator. The restrictions hampered the country's ability to defend against attacks by Russia.
Additionally, regulatory scrutiny could block chances for Musk to merge SpaceX and Tesla, an idea he has promoted, while acknowledging shareholders' approval would be required first.
SpaceX and Tesla had lost about $456 billion in market cap by the close of business on Thursday.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic to press ahead with IPO targeting $1.5tn valuation
articles.title_zh: Anthropic to press ahead with IPO targeting $1.5tn valuation
articles.content_orig:
Following tech's selloff on Wall Street this week, some investors are lowering their expectations for Anthropic.
The artificial intelligence company had been looking toward a $2 trillion valuation in its IPO up until recently, but stakeholders told CNBC that even $1.5 trillion is now in doubt, with one investor calling that number a "stretch."
Anthropic declined to comment.
The change in sentiment comes alongside growing concerns about the outsized spending by AI companies and a sharp post-midterm slump in the market. The Nasdaq plummeted more than 5% on Thursday, its steepest drop in 19 months, reflecting fears that Democrats' newfound power in Washington, D.C., and a nationwide rebuke of AI will lead to a slowdown in the buildout of data centers.
Bearishness on the AI trade was on the rise before the election. The Nasdaq suffered its worst month in October since March 2025, led by declines in chipmakers and neoclouds.
Anthropic is set to list on the Nasdaq , under the ticker ANT, and is gearing up for an expected debut in a matter of weeks. Last month, Anthropic was reportedly seeking a valuation as high as $2 trillion . As of May, the company was privately valued at $965 billion.
With the latest market turmoil, one investor said $1 trillion to $1.25 trillion is a more likely valuation target, although that could change with market conditions. The investors asked not to be named because they're not authorized to speak about the matter.
Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, told CNBC that, "Investors will expect the IPO to be priced at least at the low end of previous expectations."
"The market really needs this IPO to go well and the bankers on the deal surely understand that," Luria said. "The best way to set Anthropic up for success is to price the deal well."
The company is expected to kick off its roadshow next week.

articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices on Friday posted a steep weekly loss, as investors weighed the risk of renewed military escalation between the U.S. and Iran following the midterm elections.
International benchmark Brent crude futures added 3 cents to close at $98.32 per barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained 31 cents to settle at $90.83 per barrel. Brent fell more than 16% for the week while U.S. crude lost neary 13%.
Investors are assessing whether the conclusion of the U.S. midterm elections could pave the way for renewed actions against Iran, potentially threatening oil supplies from the Middle East.
Bob McNally, Rapidan Energy Group founder and president, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" that he sees an 80% probability of military fighting resuming, forecasting that both oil benchmarks could climb above $100 a barrel.
However, hopes for a diplomatic resolution have also emerged after Iran reportedly sent a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar, Reuters reported, citing a senior Iranian official.
Iran reported three additional attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, while data from the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) indicated that attacks on vessels were continuing at a near-record rate.
"President Donald Trump is determined, as a legacy item, almost at all costs, to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, having them give up their nuclear capabilities," McNally said.
"The Iranian regime, on the other hand, is not willing to do it. And as long as that core difference in that deal space is absent, the escalation dynamic remains in place," he added.
McNally's view is shared by other analysts, including Lombard Odier's chief economist Samy Chaar and head of investment strategy Luca Bindelli.
— CNBC's Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Why Micron’s Stock Valuation Now Looks Ridiculous
articles.title_zh: Why Micron’s Stock Valuation Now Looks Ridiculous
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Shares of memory chipmaker Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) dropped 7% on Nov. 4, ending at $795.23, and kept falling on Nov. 5. At around $690 as I write, the stock sits over 40% under the $1,213.56 it finished at on June 25, its all-time closing high.
Stocks linked to artificial intelligence data centers slid broadly on Nov. 4 after Democrats' midterm election wins, as traders prepared for a slower build-out, according to CNBC.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
When I called Micron stock a buy last week, shares had just ended at $884.74. They've since fallen over 20%. But Micron's latest outlook, issued with its results on Sept. 30, hasn't changed. That means investors can now buy the same expected earnings for less.
And I think these earnings still show a company making more money every quarter -- with a stock priced as if that's about to stop.
Micron's fiscal 2026 ended on Sept. 3, and most of its profit came late in the year. Showing how fast the memory shortage boosted results, Micron's earnings per share under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) went from $4.60 in fiscal Q1 to $12.07, $24.67 and $32.87 in the next three quarters. For the full year, GAAP earnings per share were $74.33, up from $7.59 in fiscal 2025. Revenue in fiscal Q4 alone hit $54.2 billion, up 379% year over year.
The climb hasn't stopped, but it's getting less steep. For the current quarter (the first quarter of fiscal 2027), management forecast GAAP earnings per share of $37.84, plus or minus $1. That would be around 15% over fiscal Q4, after a 33% gain the quarter before -- and more than eight times the $4.60 Micron earned in the same quarter a year earlier.
In other words, Micron expects to earn around half of fiscal 2026's per-share total in this one quarter.
Management also expects revenue to climb from the previous quarter in every quarter of fiscal 2027, with higher gross margins after this quarter.
The Nov. 4 sell-off centered on data centers, and they're Micron's largest market. Two of its four business units, core data center and cloud memory, pulled in $34.3 billion of fiscal Q4's revenue, or around 63% of the total.
Limits on new data centers have also gained ground in some states. In April, Maine's legislature passed a temporary statewide freeze on new large data centers. It would have been the first of its kind in the U.S., but the governor vetoed it.
Yes, a slower build-out might eat into demand. But a big part of Micron's sales is already spoken for. The business has signed 26 strategic customer agreements, which are multiyear take-or-pay deals (customers owe for the volumes they agreed to, even if they don't take them). Its remaining performance obligations, or the contracted sales it hasn't recognized yet from deals with set pricing terms, counted at minimum prices, totaled around $150 billion.
"[E]ven at floor prices, we expect margins meaningfully above any prior cycle peak margins," chief financial officer Mark Murphy said in prepared remarks for the Sept. 30 earnings call.
That means management thinks the contracts can shield profits even if prices fall to the bottom of the agreed ranges.
Sure, the deals don't cover it all. Micron estimates the agreements make up over 35% of its revenue through 2030, which leaves most of its sales linked to market prices.
At around $690, Micron trades at under 10 times earnings, based on the $74.33 per share it earned in fiscal 2026. At $884.74, it traded at around 12 times the same earnings.
For a business expecting to earn about half as much in one quarter, investors at that price-to-earnings ratio are arguably pricing in a big fall in profits when the shortage ends.
It could happen. Memory makers tend to add supply when prices are high, and Micron does too. It expects to spend around $25 billion on capital expenditures in just the first half of fiscal 2027 -- near the $27.4 billion it spent in all of fiscal 2026.
But management also says it doesn't yet have "line of sight to when supply and demand will return to balance." And at under 10 times earnings, the stock already allows for a sharp drop in profits.
So, I'd still buy Micron stock at this price. I'd just space my purchases out over the months ahead rather than buy all at once. A stock that lost 7% in one day on worries about a slower data center build-out might do it again.

articles.title_orig: We Energies rate hike approved, customers to pay more in 2027 and 2028
articles.title_zh: We Energies rate hike approved, customers to pay more in 2027 and 2028
articles.content_orig:
Wisconsin regulators approved another rate increase, but the final impact on customers' monthly bills has yet to be determined.
Wisconsin regulators approved another rate increase, but the final impact on customers' monthly bills has yet to be determined.
We Energies customers will see their energy bills rise over the next two years after Wisconsin regulators approved a rate increase, though the final amount has not been determined.
Preliminary estimates were released on Friday after this report aired:
The Public Service Commission of Wisconsin, a nonpartisan, three-member board, met for more than 10 hours Thursday before voting on the request. It will be the energy company’s sixth rate increase since 2020.
In April, We Energies said its proposed rate changes would increase bills by about $13 per month in 2027 and another $8 to $9 per month in 2028. The PSC did not finalize the rates Thursday.
We Energies said the increase will support “key investments,” including more Wisconsin-produced energy, continued tree trimming to reduce power outages and the placement of power lines underground to strengthen the grid against severe weather.
“Our customers count on us every day for the energy they need, and we recognize our responsibility to continue providing safe and reliable energy, while keeping customer bills as low as possible,” a We Energies spokesperson said. “During this months-long process we worked with customer groups and Commission staff to reduce costs to customers by tens of millions of dollars.”
The Citizens Utility Board of Wisconsin, an independent nonprofit consumer advocacy group, expects the increase to be less than what We Energies requested.
“Based on where [the PSC] landed on key issues, we can say with confidence that this rate hike will be well below what the utility asked for,” said Tom Content, the group’s executive director. “The savings could be in the hundreds of millions of dollars, but unfortunately not enough to stop an increase from taking effect.”
The Clean Economy Coalition of Wisconsin echoed that assessment, saying that while reducing the requested increase was “a meaningful step toward holding the utility accountable and protecting customers from excessive costs,” the decision underscored the need for stronger protections against repeated increases and broader reform.
We Energies said that regardless of the final increase, Wisconsin energy costs will remain below the national average and in line with rates elsewhere in the Midwest.
The commission’s written order, which will include the final rates, is expected in a few weeks.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia hardware worth $11.4M vanished between Oakland and Texas
articles.title_zh: Nvidia hardware worth $11.4M vanished between Oakland and Texas
articles.content_orig:
A shipment of Nvidia hardware valued at $11.4 million vanished in transport between Oakland and Texas over the summer, and more than two months later, police have announced no arrests or recovery of the cargo.
As reported by The Mercury News , six pallets of unknown Nvidia equipment left Oakland on August 29 on a truck bound for Fort Worth, Texas. The hardware was reportedly picked up as scheduled by a truck bearing the logo of a food transportation company before vanishing off the grid. The theft wasn’t noticed until early September, when the buyers realized that the shipment had never been received. Police attempting to trace the truck’s route found it had made several multi-hour stops after picking up the hardware before losing the truck somewhere in San Bernardino County, California.
Oakland police confirmed that there was a grand theft report filed on September 13 and that the investigation remains ongoing. Authorities have not said what Nvidia hardware was stolen or exactly how the theft was carried out.
The theft in Oakland is the latest in a wave of increasingly bold hardware heists. As Ars’ Ashley Belanger reported recently , thieves have made off with more than $100 million in similar shipments since June. According to investigators cited by NBC News , the criminals have shown planning and sophistication by employing techniques like GPS location spoofing and even arranging collisions with police escort vehicles. Stolen components can be stripped down and sold in gray-market transactions or shipped overseas where access to US tech hardware may be restricted.
Nvidia’s hardware has been a specific target. In 2025, police investigated burglaries of Nvidia hardware, valued at more than $7.5 million, around Fremont and Union City, California. As reported by The Mercury News , police believe the thefts were carried out by a group that obtained vehicles for the heist in Southern California before traveling north to the Bay Area.
Professor Olaf Groth of UC Berkeley’s Haas School of Business told ABC News that “if a chip costs about $550,000, then they go for about $1 million or more abroad.” Those margins, he said, may be incentivizing criminals: “Because cargoes are getting bigger. The heists are getting more complex and that will point toward a professionalization of the teams that are hijacking these.”
Not every would-be heist crew gets it right, though. A theft in September, reported by Wired , saw two trailers marked with Nvidia and PlusAI logos stolen from outside of a warehouse facility in California. The trailers were recovered by police nearby, presumably after the criminals cut the locks to reveal they were each loaded with 20,000 pounds of sand. PlusAI is a company working on autonomous trucking solutions with Nvidia, and the sand was in the trailers to simulate freight loads.

articles.title_orig: Artist pulls popular screensaver from Roku OS because of Fox acquisition
articles.title_zh: Artist pulls popular screensaver from Roku OS because of Fox acquisition
articles.content_orig:
Some Roku OS users have been sad to learn that their favorite screensaver will no longer be available as of December 1.
This week, affected users reported receiving an alert on their device that they will not be able to use the “Aquatic Life” screensaver after this month, as first reported by Cord Cutters News .
The screensaver has been an option for Roku OS users for 10 years. Roku has been licensing the animation, which is called the Marine Aquarium , from artist Jim Sachs through Prolific Publishing.
Sachs is the creator and copyright holder of the Marine Aquarium. He developed the screensaver through his company SereneScreen . He tells Ars Technica that the licensing agreement with Roku is up for renewal every October and can be canceled by either party for any reason. A day after learning that Fox was planning to buy Roku , a deal that closed today , Sachs told Prolific that he wouldn’t be renewing Roku’s license.
“I can’t be part of the Fox world,” he tells Ars, pointing to Fox News’ controversial style of news and entertainment.
Roku will automatically switch the Aquatic Life screensaver on affected devices to the Roku City screensaver, another popular animation that includes subtle advertisements , according to the user notice.
The Aquatic Life screensaver provided an ad-free, relaxing display for years for some Roku users. Numerous people online have lamented the impending loss of the screensaver for Roku OS .
“When my head is in overdrive (very often with my ADHD), this screensaver grounds me and lets me exhale and become focused with myself again. It may sound over the top, but it’s true. It takes a lot for me to chill and relax, but this Aquatic Life [screensaver] is my go to. Totally gutted 😢,” a Reddit user wrote this week.
Sachs told Ars he’s interested in placating fans of the Marine Aquarium and said Roku has asked him to restore the license. When asked what his biggest concerns about Fox buying Roku are, Sachs said:
It seems that Fox simply wants another venue for spreading their philosophy, which I consider repugnant. I can’t stand the idea of my artwork being used to lure even one person down that rabbit hole.
The decision to not renew the licensing contract has “major financial consequences,” Sachs said.
“Our needs are very small, with a high property tax bill being the only significant expense,” he said. “We’ll be okay but can’t start any of the projects I had planned.”
According to Sachs, the licensing “agreement was $80,000 per year for exclusive rights to all set-top devices, or $60,000 per year for non-exclusive. They have always opted for exclusive.” Ars asked Roku to confirm the details of the licensing agreement but didn’t hear back ahead of publication.
The licensing deal with Roku was Sachs’ primary form of income, he told Ars, noting low sales of the version of the screensaver for computers.
Marine Aquarium fans can still buy the screensaver for Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android, but it seems unlikely that it will return to the Roku platform.
“One of the best reasons to buy Roku was the themes and less ads than competitors. But they haven’t added any new themes in years aside from sponsored ones, and they increased the amount of ads,” a Reddit user posted this week in response to Roku’s loss of the Aquatic Life screensaver.
Sachs, meanwhile, says he has “no delusions” that pulling the license will have any meaningful impact. However, he’s hopeful that another streaming company will look to offer the screensaver.
“I’m assuming that Fox will not be reversing their whole rage-based business model and take responsibility for all the harm it has caused. I’d be happy to restore the license under those circumstances. They could even have it for free,” he said.
Fox closed its acquisition of Roku today for $22 billion.

articles.title_orig: After cancer surgery, Pope Leo embarks on Latin America trip with a first stop in secular Uruguay
articles.title_zh: After cancer surgery, Pope Leo embarks on Latin America trip with a first stop in secular Uruguay
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo is travelling to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru
Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.
The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".
It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.
At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".
"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.
"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."
On Friday Pope Leo presided over the annual memorial Mass for cardinals and bishops who have died
The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.
The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.
Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.
Father Fernando Laguna said his heart was filled with joy when the Pope's visit to Argentina was announced
"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.
"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"
The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.
'Welcome Pope Leo' reads this poster in the Argentinian church in Rome
This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.
But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.
The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.
"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.
Worshippers at Chiclayo cathedral in Peru were delighted when their former bishop became Pope in 2025
Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.
His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.
He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.
In all three countries, the Vatican says the Pope will have meetings with survivors of clerical sexual abuse - an issue which clouded a 2018 visit to Chile and Peru by his predecessor.
"This is how the papacy reconnects with Latin America after Francis, whose visits to the region were not always seamless," is how Professor Faggioli sees it.
He believes Pope Leo has a strong sense of the unity of the Americas as one continent. "Democracies are in trouble there, so there are so many things he can address," he suggests.
"The big question then is the United States. There's no question he wants to go. So will he travel when [President Donald] Trump is still in office? I'm sure they're thinking about this."

articles.title_zh: US labor market regains ground as job growth surges, unemployment rate falls to 4.1%
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The US added 165,000 jobs in October, blowing past economists' expectations, as the labor market showed strength despite the Federal Reserve's recent rate hikes.
The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1% even amid a slight increase in labor force participation. September's underwhelming jobs report of 29,000 additions was also revised upward to a gain of 60,000 jobs.
Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, deemed the results "a blowout" in a post on X .
Economists surveyed by Bloomberg projected a gain of about 70,000 jobs in October and saw the unemployment rate holding steady. Wage growth increased 0.4% from September, better than expectations for 0.3% month-over-month growth. Annual earnings rose 3.1%, beating expectations but likely still below the current inflation rate.
Employers added jobs in a number of sectors of the economy. Professional and business services, which had been seen as more vulnerable to AI-related disruptions, added 70,000 roles. Healthcare, long a strong spot for job growth, added a higher-than-average 42,000 positions.
Transportation and warehousing jobs rose by 25,000, and manufacturing continued to show strength with 19,000 additions.
"This is still a low-hire, low-fire market overall, but we could be seeing some green shoots on the hiring side," Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, said in a statement.
Other job market measures released earlier this week telegraphed steady hiring — though not to the extent of Friday's report blowout number. Job openings and hiring edged higher , the Labor Department's monthly Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey showed; private employers added 86,000 jobs , according to ADP; and layoff plans dropped to a three-year low while seasonal hiring ramped up.
"Consistent with prior, more partial indicators of the US labor market, the October Jobs Report came in very strong, across the board," Wharton economist Mohamed El-Erian posted on X.
The solid report will likely give the Federal Reserve more confidence to move forward with another rate hike in December . The central bank will also consider November jobs data and October's inflation figures before its Dec. 9 rate decision. Traders currently see a 77% chance of a 25 basis point rate hike next month, up from 67% on Thursday, according to CME FedWatch.
"Today's jobs report is a strong rebuttal to fears that the economy is heading into a meaningful slowdown," Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, said in a statement. "With wage growth also picking up, a December Fed hike remains firmly on the table despite the recent tightening in financial conditions."
Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance.

articles.title_orig: AI data centers took a beating in the midterm elections. A reckoning may be ahead for tech giants
articles.title_zh: AI data centers took a beating in the midterm elections. A reckoning may be ahead for tech giants
articles.content_orig:
Alpha Compute CEO Brittany Kaiser argues that common-sense regulations, not sweeping bans or moratoriums, are the key to unlocking economic growth while protecting local communities.
President Donald Trump has thrown the federal government's weight behind massive data center build-outs needed to power the country's artificial intelligence (AI) boom. But a historic Democratic sweep in Texas has put one of the nation's biggest AI infrastructure hubs under new political leadership, raising questions about the future of billions of dollars in planned investments.
The victories marked a historic midterm night for Texas Democrats, who captured the governor's mansion for the first time in more than three decades and won a U.S. Senate seat for the first time since 1988.
Texas is poised to overtake Virginia as the nation's largest data center market and is projected to account for roughly a quarter of new U.S. data center power capacity through 2030. With at least 248 projects planned across the state, investment bank Jefferies estimates that 13.3 gigawatts of announced developments could be at risk under a moratorium backed by Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa.
ONE STATE IS GROUND ZERO AS TRUMP'S MULTIBILLION-DOLLAR TECH AMBITIONS FACE A MIDTERM TEST
Texas is poised to overtake Virginia as the nation's largest data center market and is projected to account for roughly a quarter of new U.S. capacity through 2030. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
Texas was hardly alone in facing growing opposition to data center development. In Ohio, voters weighed 21 data center-related ballot questions across 18 communities in the midterm elections, more than any other state , highlighting the mounting resistance to America's rapidly expanding AI infrastructure.
The results this week are now forcing some developers to reconsider where to invest billions of dollars in future projects as political power shifts.
"It makes us and our investors pause and think if we should be investing somewhere else," Brittany Kaiser, CEO of Alpha Compute, told Fox News Digital following the Republican bloodbath in Tuesday's election.
Kaiser warned that political shifts in traditionally Republican states could push billions of dollars in planned investments elsewhere, including overseas, as companies weigh growing opposition to data center development — especially within the Democratic Party.
"There's new decision making that needs to come into play and a lot more to think about than there was before the election," she said.
IT TOOK 3 MONTHS TO GET INSIDE THIS MASSIVE TEXAS DATA CENTER — HERE’S WHAT WE SAW
A data center stores and processes the digital information that powers services people use every day. (Nathan Howard/Getty Images)
But relocating projects already underway is far more complicated, particularly when developers have secured land, negotiated power agreements and committed substantial capital.
"It's not very easy to pivot after you've already made contractual and financial commitments to these types of builds," Kaiser said.
For projects still in the pipeline, however, companies have more flexibility. Kaiser said Alpha Compute has already invested in data centers in Canada, Europe and Mexico, where regulatory approvals are more straightforward.
The backlash highlights growing tensions between Washington's push to accelerate AI development and voters' concerns about electricity costs and the impact of data centers on their communities.
Kaiser urged incoming lawmakers to strike a balance between addressing community concerns and preserving what she called "the biggest economic opportunity of our generation."
The AI boom is accelerating demand for data centers across Texas as companies seek more space, power and infrastructure to support increasingly intensive computing needs. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"It's really important, yes, to make sure that data center companies are good actors and are doing things the right way," she said, calling for "common sense legislation and regulation" that allows developers to work with lawmakers and local communities.
"If we can abide by those rules, then bans and moratoriums should not be the answer," Kaiser said. "It's just let's sensibly regulate and move forward in a way that is positively impactful for communities."
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

articles.title_orig: The Taipei Mayor Election Is Not About China - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: The Taipei Mayor Election Is Not About China - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
In October, well-known Taiwanese television host Kevin Tsai, popular on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, was spotted by the media attending a campaign event for Puma Shen, a legislator running for mayor of Taipei. Given Tsai’s popularity in China, his appearance quickly sparked criticism. The incumbent Taipei mayor, Chiang Wan-an, helped defuse the controversy by inviting Tsai to the opening of his own campaign headquarters. Three weeks after attending Shen’s campaign event, Tsai publicly stated that he had never supported Taiwanese independence and that his work required him to interact with people holding a range of political views. The following day, he attended Chiang’s campaign event.
If attending a rally is tantamount to declaring one’s support for Taiwan’s future, imagine what will be made of the November 28 vote.
Shen, the candidate of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), has spent years studying Chinese influence operations and promoting civilian preparedness in Taiwan. Chinese authorities have opened an investigation into him on allegations of secession. Chiang, the Kuomintang (KMT) incumbent, has maintained an open channel of communication between officials in Taipei and Shanghai. Beijing and Washington may be tempted to interpret a Shen victory as a vote for independence or a Chiang victory as a turn toward China. Either interpretation, however, would link a municipal election to an issue that Taipei’s voters have not been asked to vote on.
Consider an exchange during the October 31 debate between Shen and Chiang. Chiang challenged Shen to explain why two redevelopment projects, one in Datong and the other in Neihu, had stalled. Chiang attributed the delays to restrictions on building heights near Taipei’s Songshan Airport. Shen fired back with a question of his own: If city officials knew about these restrictions, why hadn’t they explained them to residents from the outset? Chiang used the exchange to question his challenger’s command of city affairs. Shen, in turn, used it to ask what good that expertise did residents if they learned about an obstacle too late to do anything about it.
The most important takeaway from their heated exchanges, however, is not what the candidates said, but what they left unsaid. China, the elephant in the room when it comes to cross-strait relations, was not raised even once as a key issue during the two-hour debate.
That encapsulates the kind of local issues Taipei voters will actually base their decision on. Some might vote for Chiang, crediting him with moving other difficult projects forward, including one at Nanjichang Night Market. Others might favor Shen’s proposal to screen older buildings for earthquake risks and to help residents arrange repairs. Two homeowners could vote for different candidates – while holding precisely the same views about China. The election night count offers no way to tell.
Taipei’s recent electoral history illustrates the limits of interpreting local elections through the lens of national politics – and vice versa. In 2022, the city elected Chiang as mayor. Just over a year later, in the presidential election, the DPP’s Lai Ching-te carried Taipei, edging out the KMT’s Hou Yu-ih by just 641 votes. Chiang’s mayoral victory would therefore have been a poor guide to the city’s presidential preferences. There is even less reason to interpret a vote in the capital as evidence of a broader change of heart across Taiwan for or against a political party – or that party’s approach to China.
True, the result will shape national politics. Winning Taipei would give Shen a larger audience for his work on civilian defense. A second term would give Chiang greater standing within the KMT to make the case for engagement with Shanghai, and possibly Beijing. Plus, the Taipei mayorship has in the past served as a launching pad for presidential ambitions. Winning office gives a politician the chance to advance causes that may have had little to do with why voters chose him.
The election’s outcome could certainly also influence cross-strait relations. During Chiang’s tenure, the Taipei–Shanghai Twin-City Forum has kept officials from the two cities in contact. A Chiang victory would give him another term to pursue those exchanges. A Shen victory would test the conditions under which they can continue. Although Shen has criticized the forum’s value, he has said he would attend if it offered practical benefits and came without political preconditions. On October 14, Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office dismissed his offer, citing his alleged support for independence.
Suppose Shen wins, repeats his offer, and finds Shanghai unwilling to meet with him. Concluding that Taipei voters chose to sever contact would erase Beijing’s role in the decision. The reverse inference – that vote for Chiang implies approval of his engagement with Chinese officials – would be equally questionable. A Taipei resident might value Chiang’s ability to keep municipal officials talking while still opposing closer political ties. Wanting the conversation with Shanghai to continue is entirely compatible with wanting Beijing to have less say in Taiwan’s affairs.
Local governance is undoubtedly important for the stability of the Taiwan Strait. Taipei’s city government, for example, helps residents prepare for an air raid, down to practicing how to reach shelter when the sirens sound. How well the city carries out that work matters regardless of which party holds power. Still, it’s not going to be an issue that is top of mind when Taipei residents fill out their ballots.
On November 28, Taipei’s voters will choose who takes responsibility for the safety of their homes, the city’s readiness for an emergency, and its dealings with Shanghai. Beijing and Washington have good reason to pay close attention to what the next mayor does with that authority. But anyone claiming a mandate for independence or unification is looking for evidence the mayoral count cannot provide.

articles.title_orig: The 'Grand Theft Auto VI' Custom In-Game Cars Have Come to Life
articles.title_zh: The 'Grand Theft Auto VI' Custom In-Game Cars Have Come to Life
articles.content_orig:
West Coast Customs helped recreate the in-game custom cars of 'Grand Theft Auto VI'
Each car comes with its own backstory, including stats, figures and details
'Grand Theft Auto VI' finally arrives on November 19
Grand Theft Auto VI is finally coming, and one of the best, most detailed components of the game is coming to life. Literally.
The iconic West Coast Customs of Los Angeles was brought in to recreate some of the most recognizable in-game cars with real life counterparts. The detail that went into replicating the replicas must have been painstaking, as we even had a bit of difficulty differentiating the in-game shots (above) from the real life photos (below).
And what’s even better is that each car is baked with stats and IRL figures, bridging their digital and real-life connections even stronger. Ever wonder what the engine was under the Coquette? Or how much horsepower the Tempesta cop car has? Check out the breakdown of each car and judge for yourself how close each car got to its in-game version.
The Grotti Cheetah is quintessentially Miami. The classic mid-engined ’90s supercar is clean, with Italian-styled lines broken only by intakes feeding a 4.9L naturally-aspirated V8. West Coast Customs lowered it on track-ready tires, gave it a “Vice City fade” paint job, and trimmed the cabin with custom-stitched Italian leather.
The Buccaneer is a fully restored 1960s lowrider with a 7.5L V8, paired with hits of mahogany and gold trim throughout. The candy apple green paint, laid down in large metallic flake, carries bespoke airbrushing and pinstripes for the ultimate custom look. Air-ride suspension and gold multi-spoke rims sit under a cream ragtop and a leather interior with zebra-print inlays, because Vice City.
Perhaps the wildest build in this list, the Emerus is a track-ready thoroughbred, with aero bodywork and fighter jet-style vents built around a twin-turbo 4.0L V8. It’s painted candy orange with an even louder orange interior to match. One of the largest aero wings on the market, plus custom suspension and racing tires, keeps it planted when you’re five-star and on the run.
The icon and probably most recognizable. The mid-engined Coquette packs a 6.2L naturally aspirated V8 we all secretly know and love. Its “Yeti Camo” livery for the game in flamingo pink and vibrant purple definitely stands out in your garage. It also gets custom rims, lowered suspension and a fully custom leather interior.
The Manana is a 1970s classic with a 7.7L V8, stripped down and rebuilt with bold, straight panels for a fresh take on donk. It’s coated in large-flake Vice City blue paint with gold bumpers and trim. A sky-high custom suspension sits on oversized gold-and-chrome rims, and the matching blue leather cabin is edged in gold for added flair.
The aggressive, mid-engined Invetero Tempesta runs a flame-spitting 4.0L naturally aspirated V10. It wears a Vice Beach Police Department livery over lowered suspension and custom rims, because even one time deserve some style. Inside, the cockpit takes after a fighter jet, packed with custom leather, buttons and cutting edge police tech. All we have to say is: good luck.
Grand Theft Auto VI arrives on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S on November 19.

articles.content_orig:
Retail traders dumped the most stocks in a single day since the Covid pandemic, amid Thursday's massive tech selloff, according to Vanda Research.
Retail investors sold a net $338 million of single stocks on Thursday, with not even an hour into the close, which the market research firm noted was the largest one-day outflow since March 2020 for a group that has been known to buy the dip and keep cash within the market.
The selling comes amid a massive stock market drawdown as traders rotated out of technology. On Thursday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average plummeted 1,800 points, effectively erasing any post-midterm bump, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped into a correction.
"On a typical sell-off, retail buy the dip," read a note from the firm. "Today, that bid has effectively disappeared from individual names."
The firm noted that what buying remained has been concentrated in leveraged vehicles such as the ProShares UltraPro QQQ (TQQQ), which delivers three times the performance in the Nasdaq-100 index, and the Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X Shares (SOXL), which is supposed to track moves in semiconductors.
"This looks like a rare buyers' strike colliding with forced selling," read the note.
— CNBC's Nick Wells contributed to this story.
(Correction: Fixes day of the week in first paragraph.)

articles.title_orig: Protesters break into Microsoft data center site in Amsterdam as Europe’s backlash spreads
articles.title_zh: Protesters break into Microsoft data center site in Amsterdam as Europe’s backlash spreads
articles.content_orig:
Protesters in the Netherlands have broken into a construction site for a new Microsoft data centre in Amsterdam, the latest action in a growing movement sweeping Europe.
Several hundred activists occupied the site in the Sloterdijk district on Friday, responding to a call for a two-day protest across Europe against data centres, which handle the large processing workloads associated with artificial intelligence (AI). Demonstrators clashed with police as some climbed a crane and set off flares.
Nathan Timmer, of the protest group Geef Tegengas – which translates as Push Back – told local broadcaster AT5 that demonstrators were occupying the site in an effort to stop construction.
“We don’t want it to be built. Nobody needs it,” Timmer said. “The only thing this will be used for is AI slop. AI warfare, data surveillance and committing genocide. We don’t want that.”
Pro-Palestinian activists also joined the demonstrations in the Dutch capital. By late afternoon police were escorting activists off the construction site, though some remained, local media reported.
Dutch police said they detained 150-200 people suspected of trespassing during the protest.
Microsoft said it was aware of the Amsterdam demonstration.
“We understand that people feel strongly about the project, and we respect their right to express those views peacefully,” a spokesperson said. “However, we do not condone any actions that are unlawful or that put people’s safety at risk.”
Data centres face resistance around the world due to the massive amounts of computing power and water they use. Activists argue that the boom in facilities serving cloud computing and AI is moving faster than public consultation and environmental oversight.
Dozens of civil society and grassroots groups have said they will join the “Stop Dirty Data Centres” events on Friday and Saturday in 15 European countries, including Ireland, Poland, Denmark, Finland, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, France and the United Kingdom, organisers said.
In Germany, a dozen protesters gathered in front of a data centre on the outskirts of Berlin on Friday.
“We want to put a stop to this blind construction of data centres around Germany, regardless of any environmental concerns,” said protest spokeswoman Caro Weber. “This is really, really dangerous for our future.”
About 100 people also protested against data centres in front of the Polish parliament, representing communities around Warsaw where new centres are planned.
In Italy, the fast-growing data centre industry is facing an equally rapid rise in grassroots opposition, particularly in the northern Lombardy region, the country’s main hub for digital infrastructure.

articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.
Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.
Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers. Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.
As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent. Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works toward a particular goal on your behalf.
For instance, if you wanted to plan a vacation, you could open a new Space focused on that particular project, and whenever you want to work on it with Muse, you would click to open that particular tab. Or, if you’re focused on collecting recipes for an upcoming family event, you’d open a new Space for that particular project. Other examples Meta gives are a holiday gift tracker, a wedding planner, or a space for DIY projects.
“Describe an idea in chat, and Muse builds a space for you, whether that’s a tracker, a planner or a project board,” Meta says.
Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.
“Connect the apps you use, and your spaces keep themselves up to date in the background, so new concert dates, price changes, or savings progress show up without you having to ask,” the company says.
On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it. I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard. Excited to see what you build.”
Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months. During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.
The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents. Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week. On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice , which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.
The company is in competition with other cute and cuddly AI agents — including OpenAI’s dots and SpaceXAI’s Grokbot , which were debuted with similarly cartoonish personas.

articles.title_orig: Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
articles.title_zh: Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
articles.content_orig:
Is the artificial intelligence (AI) gold rush coming to an end, or is this simply a reality check?
That's the question which is hanging over investors, and which has prompted steep falls on the world's stock markets.
The sell-off in the US on Thursday was most dramatic on the Nasdaq, home to tech industry titans such as Alphabet, Nvidia, Meta and Apple.
It followed sweeping gains by the Democrats in this week's midterm elections in the US, which have given the party full control of Congress.
A number of leading Democrats campaigned against the unhindered expansion of data centres, which have underpinned the growth of artificial intelligence.
Fears this will lead to more regulation of AI appear to have concerned investors. But worries about the industry's prospects have been growing for some time.
The release of Chat GPT by Open AI in late 2022 is widely seen as having generated massive public and corporate interest in the practical uses of AI. It also sparked a modern-day gold rush.
Investors flocked to put their money into companies producing computer chips and  networking infrastructure, building data centres and providing the energy to power them, as well as developing the AI itself. The value of tech companies soared.
The boom continued into this year. Investments in AI are expected to reach $1trillion in 2026 alone according to research by Goldman Sachs. The sector has scooped up so much available cash that other industries have seen their own borrowing costs increase as a result.
But investors want returns, and in recent months concerns have been growing about whether the AI boom can produce the expected riches.
Those worries have emerged at a time when public comments from AI researchers casting doubt over the safety of artificial intelligence - even suggesting it could represent an existential threat to humanity - have been grabbing headlines and fuelling speculation that a clampdown could lie ahead.
While the Trump administration has been all-in on AI, or "super intelligence" as the president likes to call it, many leading Democrats tapped into grassroots concerns about the expansion of data centres and their impact on local communities.
These were largely focused on the facilities' high consumption of water and electricity, which many feared would push up their household bills – as well as the noise, use of land, and general disruption associated with them.
A Gallup poll published in May showed 71% of Americans would oppose the building of a data centre in their community. The figure for a nuclear power station was 53%.
James Talarico, who won the Senate race in once staunchly Republican Texas, was one of those to respond to this scepticism.
"While we want to protect America's leadership in artificial intelligence, we are still grappling with how it will affect everything from how we work to how our children learn," he said.
"We must protect Americans and establish clear, consistent laws for businesses."
With control of both houses of Congress, Democrats are now expected to challenge the president's technology agenda more vigorously, while introducing legislation which could curb the expansion of the industry.
Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned against data centres, pledging a moratorium on the construction of new facilities.
Hinojosa's win could present opposition to tech multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who has moved large parts of SpaceX and Tesla's operations to the state, for years a Republican stronghold.
The Tesla boss had spent nearly $450m to back Republican campaigns in the midterms.
As the co-founder of the British-based technology firm Arm Holdings, Tudor Brown, points out, "stock values are based on future earnings not present earnings". If the rewards are not likely to be as great as expected, some investors will choose to sell up.
The falls seen on stock markets over the past 24 hours would appear to have been triggered by the midterm results. But concerns that tech firms have become overvalued were being expressed long before the elections.
The question now is whether this is simply the removal of froth from an over-exuberant market, or a sign that the AI rush is a bubble about to burst, with much wider consequences.
Nandini Roy Choudhury of Future Market Insights thinks investors will assess whether the political shift could result in restrictions on data centre construction, energy consumption and the deployment of AI technology.
She adds there is unlikely to be an immediate widespread recovery in tech stocks as traders are likely to be more selective, favouring firms with stronger balance sheets.
Brown thinks the impact will be limited. Share valuations, he thinks, were inflated by expectations of "almost infinite AI growth", which have been followed by "a bit of a panic".
"There is a natural floor to this", he says. "After that it will reflect I think that actually there's still a lot of money being made in these companies".
